title: Railways
tagline: From horse-drawn coal carts to trains that float on magnets
intro: Imagine a world where the fastest way to travel over land was the speed of a galloping horse, and a trip across a country took weeks. Then, in about one human lifetime, iron rails and puffing steam engines changed everything. In these 20 parts you will ride the whole story: wooden wagonways in coal mines, Richard Trevithick's first steam locomotive, George and Robert Stephenson's famous Rocket, and the world's first proper intercity railway. You will learn exactly how a steam engine pushes a train and why wheels stay on the track. Then we cross continents on the transcontinental railroads, discover how trains invented time zones, plunge underground on the first subways, and switch to electric and diesel power. We will look honestly at accidents, hard labour and harm railways caused, before boarding bullet trains, floating maglevs and the trains of the future. All aboard!

outline.title: Before the Rails
covers: How people and goods moved over land before railways: walking, pack animals, carts on muddy rutted roads, and boats on rivers
Why heavy loads like coal, stone and grain were so slow and expensive to move by road
The Diolkos in ancient Greece (around 600 BCE): a paved trackway with grooves used to drag ships and cargo across the Isthmus of Corinth — an early 'guided way', not a railway with engines
Wheel ruts and grooved roads in the ancient world, and why a smooth fixed path makes pulling easier (less friction, less sinking into mud)
Mining carts in central Europe in the 1500s that ran on wooden planks, shown in Georgius Agricola's book De re metallica (1556)
The big idea of the whole story: a smooth track lets one horse (and later one engine) pull far more weight
keyFacts: The Diolkos across the Isthmus of Corinth was about 6–8.5 km long and was used for centuries, starting around 600 BCE
Agricola's De re metallica was published in 1556, a year after his death, and includes pictures of mine carts guided along planks
On a good smooth track a horse can pull many times more weight than it can on a rough dirt road
outline.hook: End in the coalfields of England, where miners were about to lay wooden rails above ground for the first time.

outline.title: Wooden Rails and Horse Power
covers: The Wollaton Wagonway in Nottinghamshire (around 1603–1604), built by Huntingdon Beaumont, often called the first overland wagonway in England
The wagonways of north-east England around Newcastle, carrying coal from mines to ships on the River Tyne; horses pulling wagons on wooden rails
The Tanfield Arch (built 1725–1727), thought to be the oldest surviving railway bridge in the world
The switch to iron: cast iron plates on rails at Coalbrookdale around 1767, then L-shaped 'plateways' and later edge rails with flanged wheels
The Surrey Iron Railway (opened 1803), a horse-drawn public railway that anyone could pay to use
The Swansea and Mumbles Railway, which began carrying fare-paying passengers in horse-drawn carriages in 1807
keyFacts: The Wollaton Wagonway was about 3 km (2 miles) long
The Surrey Iron Railway opened in 1803 between Wandsworth and Croydon, south of London
The Swansea and Mumbles Railway began the world's first known regular fare-paying passenger railway service in 1807, pulled by horses
outline.hook: End by asking: what if something stronger than a horse — something that never got tired — could pull the wagons?

outline.title: Taming Steam
covers: Thomas Newcomen's atmospheric steam engine (1712), used to pump water out of mines; it was huge, slow and stood still
James Watt's separate condenser (patented 1769), which made steam engines far more efficient — but Watt preferred low-pressure engines and was wary of high-pressure steam
Nicolas-Joseph Cugnot's steam-powered road vehicle in France (around 1769–1770), built to pull cannons; it was slow and hard to steer
William Murdoch's small model steam carriage (1780s)
Why high-pressure steam was the key to a moving engine: a smaller, lighter engine could produce lots of power
Simple science: water boils into steam that takes up much more space, and that expanding steam can push a piston
keyFacts: Newcomen's first known working engine was installed in 1712 near Dudley in the English Midlands
Watt's patent for the separate condenser was granted in 1769
When water turns to steam at normal air pressure, it expands to about 1,600 times its volume
outline.hook: End in Cornwall with a strong, daring young engineer who was not afraid of high-pressure steam: Richard Trevithick.

outline.title: Trevithick's Iron Horse
covers: Richard Trevithick, Cornish mining engineer, and his high-pressure 'puffer' engines
His 'Puffing Devil' road locomotive that climbed Camborne Hill on Christmas Eve 1801 — and was later destroyed by fire when left unattended
The Penydarren locomotive in South Wales, 21 February 1804: the first known steam locomotive to haul a load on rails, winning a bet for ironmaster Samuel Homfray
The problem: the heavy engine cracked the brittle cast-iron plate rails
'Catch Me Who Can' (1808), a locomotive running on a circular track in London where people paid to ride
Why Trevithick did not get rich: money troubles, broken rails, and moving on to other projects (he later went to South America)
keyFacts: On 21 February 1804 the Penydarren locomotive pulled about 10 tons of iron and around 70 men nearly 10 miles (about 16 km) from Penydarren to Abercynon
That journey took a little over 4 hours, including stops to clear the track
Catch Me Who Can ran in 1808 near Euston in London; a ride cost one shilling
outline.hook: End by saying Trevithick had shown it could be done — now coal-mine engineers in northern England would make it work every day.

outline.title: The Colliery Engines
covers: Matthew Murray and John Blenkinsop's Salamanca (1812) on the Middleton Railway in Leeds, using a toothed rack rail and cog wheel — the first commercially successful steam locomotive
William Hedley, Timothy Hackworth and Jonathan Forster's Puffing Billy (built around 1813–1814) at Wylam Colliery, which proved smooth iron wheels on smooth rails had enough grip
George Stephenson: a self-taught engine-wright who could not read until his late teens; his first locomotive Blücher at Killingworth (1814)
Improving rails: wrought-iron rails (patented by John Birkinshaw in 1820) that were much less brittle than cast iron
Stephenson's safety lamp for miners (1815), invented around the same time as Humphry Davy's — a fair look at a rival claim
Why coal mines were the perfect place for early locomotives: short tracks, heavy loads and plenty of fuel
keyFacts: Salamanca began work in 1812 on the Middleton Railway, which still runs today as a heritage railway
Puffing Billy is the oldest surviving steam locomotive in the world and is displayed at the Science Museum in London
Stephenson's Blücher first ran on 25 July 1814
outline.hook: End with a Quaker businessman in Darlington looking for a cheaper way to move coal to the river at Stockton.

outline.title: Stockton & Darlington: A Railway for the Public
covers: Edward Pease, the Quaker financier who backed the line, and Parliament's Act approving it (1821)
George Stephenson as engineer, and his choice of track gauge of 4 ft 8½ in (1,435 mm), taken from the colliery wagonways he knew
Robert Stephenson & Company, the world's first factory built to make locomotives, founded in Newcastle in 1823
Opening day, 27 September 1825: Locomotion No. 1, driven by George Stephenson, pulling coal wagons and hundreds of passengers
How the line really worked at first: steam engines pulled coal, but most passengers rode in horse-drawn coaches; stationary engines hauled wagons up slopes
Its importance: the first public railway to use steam locomotives
keyFacts: The Stockton and Darlington Railway opened on 27 September 1825 (its 200th anniversary was celebrated in 2025)
The main line was about 26 miles (about 40 km) long
4 ft 8½ in (1,435 mm) later became the 'standard gauge' used by about half the world's railways
outline.hook: End with merchants in Liverpool and Manchester deciding to build something bigger — but first they needed to choose which engine was best.

outline.title: The Rainhill Trials and the Rocket
covers: Why the Liverpool & Manchester directors held a competition: some wanted stationary engines and cables instead of locomotives
The rules and the £500 prize; the crowds of spectators at Rainhill near Liverpool

The contestants: Rocket (George and Robert Stephenson, with Henry Booth), Novelty (John Braithwaite and John Ericsson), Sans Pareil (Timothy Hackworth), Perseverance (Timothy Burstall) and Cycloped (powered by a horse on a treadmill!)
What happened: Novelty was fast and a crowd favourite but broke down; Sans Pareil cracked a cylinder; Rocket completed the trials
Rocket's clever design: a multi-tubular boiler (many copper fire-tubes), a separate firebox, and a blastpipe that blasted exhaust steam up the chimney to draw the fire
Fair credit: Robert Stephenson did much of Rocket's design; Henry Booth suggested the multi-tube boiler; the blastpipe idea had earlier users
keyFacts: The Rainhill Trials took place from 6 to 14 October 1829
Rocket reached a top speed of about 30 mph (about 48 km/h), astonishing for the time
Rocket's boiler had 25 copper fire-tubes; the original Rocket is preserved and displayed in Britain
outline.hook: End with Rocket preparing for opening day of the new railway — a day of triumph that would also bring tragedy.

outline.title: The First Modern Railway
covers: The Liverpool & Manchester Railway, opened 15 September 1830: the first intercity railway with double track, timetables, tickets, and only steam locomotives — for both passengers and freight
Engineering feats: crossing the boggy Chat Moss on a floating bed of brushwood and earth, the Olive Mount cutting and the Sankey Viaduct
Opening day: the Duke of Wellington attends; MP William Huskisson is struck by Rocket and dies that evening — one of the first widely reported railway passenger deaths
The surprise success: far more passengers than expected; travel time between the cities dropped dramatically
Railway Mania in 1840s Britain: hundreds of companies, investors getting rich and losing fortunes; George Hudson, the 'Railway King'
Isambard Kingdom Brunel's Great Western Railway with broad 7 ft ¼ in gauge, the 'Gauge War', and the Gauge Act of 1846
keyFacts: The Liverpool & Manchester Railway was about 35 miles (56 km) long and opened on 15 September 1830
In 1846 alone Parliament approved over 250 new railway Acts during Railway Mania
Brunel's broad gauge was finally converted to standard gauge in May 1892
outline.hook: End by inviting the reader to climb onto the footplate and see how a steam locomotive actually works.

outline.title: Inside a Steam Locomotive
covers: The firebox: burning coal (or wood or oil) heats water; the fireman shovels coal while the driver controls the engine
The boiler and fire-tubes: hot gases pass through tubes surrounded by water, turning lots of water to steam quickly
The regulator (throttle), cylinders and pistons: steam pushes a piston back and forth; connecting rods turn the driving wheels
Valve gear: lets steam in on alternate sides of the piston and lets the driver go forward, backward, or use steam more efficiently
The blastpipe and chimney: exhaust steam makes the 'chuff' sound and pulls air through the fire; the safety valve stops the boiler bursting
Tenders and water: why steam engines needed frequent water stops, and water troughs that let trains scoop water at speed
Why a steam engine wastes most of its fuel's energy, and why that matters later in the story
keyFacts: Typical steam locomotives turned only around 5–10% of the energy in their coal into useful pulling work
Big steam locomotives could use thousands of litres of water per hour
The Mallard set the world speed record for steam of 126 mph (203 km/h) on 3 July 1938
outline.hook: End with a question: the engine can push, but what keeps a heavy train on two thin rails, even around curves?

outline.title: Rails, Wheels, Bridges and Tunnels
covers: Steel wheel on steel rail: very low rolling friction, so little energy is needed to keep a heavy load moving
Flanges and coned (slightly sloped) wheel treads: how wheelsets steer themselves and stay centred, and why flanges are a backup, not the main steering
Gauge, sleepers (ties), ballast, and points (switches) that move trains from one track to another
Why railways need gentle slopes and wide curves; cuttings, embankments and viaducts; rack (cog) railways for steep mountains
Famous engineering: Brunel's Box Tunnel (1841), the Forth Bridge (1890), the Gotthard Tunnel in Switzerland (1882)
Signals and the 'block' idea: only one train allowed in a section of track at a time
keyFacts: A steel wheel on a steel rail has much lower rolling resistance than a rubber tyre on a road — a key reason trains are so efficient
Most main-line railways keep slopes gentle, often less than about 2% (2 metres up for every 100 metres along)
The Forth Bridge in Scotland opened in 1890 and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site
outline.hook: End by crossing the Atlantic, where a young country with vast distances was hungry for railways.

outline.title: Rails Across America
covers: The Baltimore & Ohio Railroad (chartered 1827), with the first stone laid on 4 July 1828 by Charles Carroll, the last living signer of the Declaration of Independence
Peter Cooper's Tom Thumb and its famous race with a horse-drawn car in 1830 — the horse won after a belt slipped, but the engine impressed everyone
The Best Friend of Charleston (1830), which ran the first regularly scheduled steam passenger service in the US, and its boiler explosion in 1831 after the safety valve was held down
American changes to British designs: the cowcatcher (pilot), big headlamps, bells, and swivelling front wheels (bogies) for sharp curves
Railroads and the US Civil War: the North had far more track, and trains moved troops and supplies; Abraham Lincoln signs the Pacific Railway Act (1862)
The Underground Railroad: explain clearly it was NOT a real railway but a secret network helping enslaved people escape, using railway code words
keyFacts: Tom Thumb's race with a horse took place in August 1830
In 1861 the Northern states had roughly 22,000 miles of railroad and the Southern states roughly 9,000
The Pacific Railway Act was signed by President Lincoln on 1 July 1862
outline.hook: End with two companies, one starting in California and one on the Missouri River, racing to meet in the middle.

outline.title: Spanning Continents
covers: The first US transcontinental railroad: the Central Pacific building east from Sacramento and the Union Pacific building west from Omaha

The workers: thousands of Chinese immigrants (most of the Central Pacific's workforce) blasting tunnels through the Sierra Nevada for lower pay than white workers; Irish immigrants and Civil War veterans on the Union Pacific; many died
Key people: engineer Theodore Judah, the Central Pacific's 'Big Four' including Leland Stanford, and the Union Pacific's Thomas Durant and Grenville Dodge
The Golden Spike ceremony at Promontory Summit, Utah, on 10 May 1869, and the one-word telegraph message 'DONE'
The terrible cost for Native American nations: land taken, treaties broken, and the near-destruction of the bison herds
Other great lines: Canadian Pacific (last spike 7 November 1885), and the Trans-Siberian Railway in Russia (begun 1891, completed 1916)
keyFacts: The transcontinental line from Omaha/Council Bluffs to Sacramento was about 1,900 miles (about 3,000 km) long
A trip across the US fell from many weeks or months to about a week
The Trans-Siberian Railway from Moscow to Vladivostok is about 9,289 km long — the longest railway line in the world
outline.hook: End with a puzzle: if a train leaves one town at 12 noon, what time is it in the next town? Nobody could agree — and trains were about to fix that.

outline.title: How Trains Invented Time Zones
covers: Local 'sun time': every town set its clocks by the Sun, so Bristol was about 10 minutes behind London
Confusing timetables and the danger of trains on the same track using different times
'Railway time' in Britain: the Great Western Railway used London (Greenwich) time from 1840, most railways followed by 1847, and it became the law in 1880; Bradshaw's railway guides
The 'Day of Two Noons', 18 November 1883, when US and Canadian railroads switched to standard time zones
Sandford Fleming, Canadian railway engineer who promoted worldwide standard time, and the International Meridian Conference of 1884 that chose Greenwich as the prime meridian
How the telegraph sent exact time signals along railway lines; US government made time zones law only in 1918
keyFacts: Bristol's local time was about 10 minutes behind London's
Before 1883, US railroads used dozens of different local times
The International Meridian Conference met in Washington, DC in October 1884 with delegates from 25 countries
outline.hook: End by noting that faster, busier, more punctual trains also meant bigger dangers — and inventors raced to make railways safer.

outline.title: Danger, Brakes and Safety
covers: Early dangers: boiler explosions, collisions, broken bridges, and railway workers losing fingers and lives coupling wagons by hand
Disasters that changed the rules: the Tay Bridge collapse in Scotland (28 December 1879) and the Armagh crash in Ireland (12 June 1889), which led to laws requiring continuous automatic brakes
George Westinghouse's air brake (first patent 1869; automatic version 1872): if the train splits apart, the brakes come on by themselves
Eli Janney's automatic knuckle coupler (patented 1873) and the US Safety Appliance Act of 1893
Telegraph and signal boxes, interlocking levers that stopped signalmen setting conflicting routes, and the block system
Railway workers' lives: long hours, unions and strikes such as the Pullman Strike of 1894
keyFacts: About 75 people died when the Tay Bridge collapsed under a train during a storm in 1879
The Armagh disaster of 1889 killed 80 people, many of them children on a Sunday school outing
The US Safety Appliance Act of 1893 required air brakes and automatic couplers on trains
outline.hook: End by stepping off the dangerous footplate and into a passenger carriage, to see how ordinary life was changed by railways.

outline.title: How Railways Changed Everyday Life
covers: Fresh food and milk reaching cities, newspapers and post delivered across the country overnight, and refrigerated wagons
Holidays and day trips: Thomas Cook's first railway excursion (1841) and seaside resorts; suburbs and commuting

Comfort on board: Pullman sleeping and dining cars; Pullman porters, who were Black men facing low pay and discrimination, and their union led by A. Philip Randolph (Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters, founded 1925)
Railways and empire: the first passenger train in India (Bombay to Thane, 16 April 1853), built mainly to serve British colonial interests, yet becoming part of Indian life
Railways in war: moving armies in the US Civil War and the First World War
Railways inspiring other inventions and ideas: big companies, standard parts, the telegraph network, and train-themed art, songs and stories
keyFacts: Thomas Cook's first excursion on 5 July 1841 took about 500 people from Leicester to Loughborough
India's first passenger train ran about 34 km (21 miles) from Bombay (Mumbai) to Thane on 16 April 1853
By 1900 the United States had roughly 190,000–200,000 miles of railroad track
outline.hook: End underground, in the smoky tunnels beneath London, where a new problem needed a new kind of power.

outline.title: Going Underground and Going Electric
covers: London's Metropolitan Railway (opened 10 January 1863), the world's first underground railway — using steam locomotives in 'cut-and-cover' tunnels
Werner von Siemens's small electric train at the Berlin trade exhibition (1879), and early electric trams; Volk's Electric Railway in Brighton (1883), still running
The City & South London Railway (1890): the first deep-level 'tube' railway worked by electric trains
Frank Sprague's electric streetcars in Richmond, Virginia (1888) and his multiple-unit control (1897), letting many carriages each have motors controlled from one cab
How an electric train works: power from a third rail or overhead wire (via a pantograph), traction motors turning the wheels, no smoke at the train
Subways spread: Budapest (1896), Boston (1897), Paris Métro (1900), New York (1904), Moscow (1935)
keyFacts: About 38,000 passengers rode the Metropolitan Railway on its first day in 1863
The City & South London Railway opened to the public in December 1890
New York's first subway line opened on 27 October 1904
outline.hook: End above ground, where an engine invented by a German engineer named Rudolf Diesel was about to challenge the mighty steam locomotive.

outline.title: Diesel Power and the End of Steam
covers: Rudolf Diesel's engine (patent 1892, first working engine 1897), which ignites fuel using the heat of squeezed air
How a diesel-electric locomotive works: the diesel engine runs a generator, which powers electric motors on the axles
Streamliners: Germany's 'Flying Hamburger' (1933) and the Burlington Zephyr's dawn-to-dusk run from Denver to Chicago (26 May 1934)
Steam's last glory: Mallard's 126 mph record (1938) and giants like Union Pacific's Big Boy (1941); why railways still switched (less maintenance, no water stops, one crew could run several units)
The end of mainline steam: largely complete in the US by around 1960; British Rail's last mainline steam train ran in August 1968
Decline: cars, highways and airliners take passengers away; the Beeching cuts in Britain (1960s); Amtrak formed in the US (1971); and the rise of container freight trains
keyFacts: The Burlington Zephyr ran about 1,015 miles from Denver to Chicago in about 13 hours on 26 May 1934, averaging around 77 mph
Diesel-electric locomotives turn roughly 30–40% of their fuel's energy into useful work, several times better than steam
Following the 1963 Beeching report, Britain closed thousands of miles of lines and more than 2,000 stations
outline.hook: End with trains seeming old-fashioned — until Japan unveiled something that looked like it came from the future.

outline.title: Bullet Trains
covers: Japan's Tōkaidō Shinkansen opening on 1 October 1964, just before the Tokyo Olympics; Shinji Sogō (head of Japanese National Railways) and chief engineer Hideo Shima
What makes high-speed rail possible: new dedicated tracks with gentle curves, overhead electric power, streamlined noses, signals shown inside the cab, and automatic train control
The Shinkansen's remarkable safety and punctuality record
France's TGV (1981) and its world wheel-on-rail speed record of 574.8 km/h in 2007; Germany's ICE (1991); Spain's AVE (1992)
The Channel Tunnel and Eurostar (1994), and other record tunnels: Seikan (1988) and Gotthard Base (2016)
China's high-speed rail boom from 2008, building the largest high-speed network in the world
keyFacts: The first Shinkansen trains ran at up to 210 km/h (130 mph) between Tokyo and Shin-Osaka, a distance of about 515 km
The TGV set the world speed record for a conventional (wheel-on-rail) train of 574.8 km/h on 3 April 2007
The Gotthard Base Tunnel in Switzerland, opened in 2016, is about 57 km long — the world's longest railway tunnel
China had more than 40,000 km of high-speed railway by the early 2020s, more than the rest of the world combined
outline.hook: End by asking: if wheels have a speed limit, what if a train had no wheels touching the track at all?

outline.title: Maglev and the Trains of Tomorrow
covers: Maglev science: magnets that repel or attract lift the train a few centimetres, and a linear motor in the guideway pushes it along — no wheel friction
Pioneers: Hermann Kemper's German patent (1934) and Eric Laithwaite's work on linear motors in Britain; the small Birmingham Airport maglev (1984)
The Shanghai Maglev (opened 2002–2004), the first high-speed commercial maglev; Japan's superconducting SCMaglev and its 603 km/h record (2015); the delayed Chūō Shinkansen
Why maglev is rare: very expensive special guideways that can't connect to normal tracks
Hype versus reality: the Hyperloop idea (2013) and why companies like Hyperloop One shut down (2023)
Cleaner trains for a warming planet: electrification, battery trains, hydrogen trains (first passenger service in Germany, 2018), driverless metros, and smart signalling
keyFacts: Japan's L0 Series SCMaglev reached 603 km/h (375 mph) on 21 April 2015, the fastest speed ever by a train
The Shanghai Maglev runs about 30 km between the city and Pudong Airport in roughly 7–8 minutes
Per passenger, an electric train typically produces far less carbon dioxide than a car or a plane on the same trip
outline.hook: End by looking back down the long line of track — from horses on wooden rails to floating trains — and getting ready for the final stop.

outline.title: End of the Line? The Big Picture
covers: A quick timeline recap: wagonways, Trevithick, Rocket, Liverpool & Manchester, the transcontinentals, time zones, subways, diesel, Shinkansen, maglev
The big ideas that stayed the same for 400 years: a smooth guided track, low friction, and pulling lots of weight with little energy
How railways shaped the modern world: cities, time, trade, holidays, big business, and other inventions
Remembering the costs honestly: workers who died, peoples whose lands were taken, accidents, pollution — and the lessons learned about safety
Railways today: billions of passenger journeys each year, huge freight trains, and fans who keep heritage steam lines running
A closing challenge for young inventors: what would YOU design for the railways of 2100?
keyFacts: The world has roughly 1 million km of railway track in total
Standard gauge — 1,435 mm, chosen by George Stephenson from colliery wagonways — is used by about 55% of the world's railways
Railways went from about 5 mph in 1804 to over 600 km/h in 2015 — in a little over 200 years
outline.hook: Finish with an inspiring final line about the next great journey being invented by someone reading this right now.

glossary: wagonway — an early track of wooden (later iron) rails on which horses pulled wagons, mostly carrying coal
plateway — an early iron track made of L-shaped plates that guided plain wheels
locomotive — a vehicle with its own engine that pulls (or pushes) a train
gauge — the distance between the inner edges of the two rails; standard gauge is 4 ft 8½ in (1,435 mm)
flange — the raised lip on the inside edge of a train wheel that stops it slipping off the rail
boiler — the tank in a steam engine where water is heated into steam
firebox — the box where the fuel is burned in a steam locomotive
piston and cylinder — steam pushes a piston to and fro inside a cylinder, and rods turn this into wheels going round
blastpipe — a pipe that shoots used steam up the chimney, pulling air through the fire to make it burn hotter
tender — the wagon behind a steam locomotive that carries its coal and water
points (switches) — movable rails that steer a train from one track onto another
signal — a light or arm beside the track telling the driver whether it is safe to go
block system — a safety method that allows only one train in each section ('block') of track at a time
air brake — brakes worked by compressed air, which come on automatically if the train splits apart
standard time / time zone — a region where everyone uses the same clock time, instead of local Sun time
third rail / overhead line — ways of feeding electricity to an electric train, either from an extra rail or from wires above
pantograph — the folding arm on the roof of an electric train that touches the overhead wire
diesel-electric — a locomotive whose diesel engine powers a generator, which runs electric motors that turn the wheels
high-speed rail — trains running at about 250 km/h or more, usually on specially built tracks
maglev — short for 'magnetic levitation': a train lifted and pushed along by magnets instead of rolling on wheels
doNotSay: Do NOT say George Stephenson invented the steam locomotive or that Rocket was the first locomotive — Trevithick's locomotive ran in 1804, and Salamanca and Puffing Billy came before Rocket
Do NOT say Stephenson's Rocket was designed by George alone — Robert Stephenson led much of the design and Henry Booth suggested the multi-tube boiler
Do NOT say the standard gauge comes directly from the width of Roman chariots — that is a popular myth; it came from the gauge of north-east England colliery wagonways that Stephenson used
Do NOT say Huskisson was the first person ever killed by a railway — say he was one of the first widely reported railway passenger deaths
Do NOT say doctors 'proved' people would suffocate or their bodies would melt at 30 mph — claims like this are mostly unsupported legends; if mentioned, label them as stories
Do NOT say Tom Thumb beat the horse — the horse won the 1830 race after the engine's belt slipped
Do NOT say the Golden Spike is still in the track — it was removed right after the ceremony and is kept at Stanford University's Cantor Arts Center

Do NOT say the transcontinental railroad was built mostly by white American workers or ignore Chinese workers — Chinese immigrants were the majority of the Central Pacific's workforce, and they were paid less
Do NOT say the Underground Railroad was a real railway or tunnel system
Do NOT say governments invented time zones — railways created standard time first; US law followed in 1918
Do NOT say Mussolini 'made the trains run on time' as fact — it was propaganda
Do NOT say the Shinkansen has never had an accident — say it has had no passenger deaths from derailments or collisions in normal service (a 2004 earthquake derailment caused no injuries)
Do NOT say maglev trains float with no power using ordinary fridge-style magnets — they need powerful electromagnets or superconducting magnets and a powered guideway
Do NOT say Hyperloop is a working form of transport — no passenger hyperloop has ever entered service
Do NOT give exact numbers of workers who died building the transcontinental or other railways as if certain — records are incomplete; say 'many' or 'hundreds or more'
